Architecture

Rethinking state management for large Angular apps

Angel Fraga·Sep 18, 2026·12 min read
ANGULAR
STATE

For years the default answer to "how do we share state?" in Angular was a store library. Those tools earned their place, but as applications grow they quietly push complexity into places you stop noticing — until you do. This post is about what that looks like and what a signals-first default can do instead.

I'm not arguing stores have no role. But the interesting question is what small fraction of your app actually needs one. Most state is local to a component tree, and treating it all the same way is where the cost creeps in.

Where stores start to hurt

A store starts honest: one well-typed action, one selector, an easy unit test. After a few features, the action count explodes, selectors fan out across feature modules, and every screen now imports a dependency nobody can fully hold in their head.

The most expensive line of code you can write is an artificial boundary that makes a two-file problem into a fifty-file problem.

None of this is anyone's fault. It's the natural shape of a global namespace: convenient at the edges, expensive in the middle.

A signals-first default

Angular's signals give you fine-grained reactivity with plain semantics. Component state stays co-located with the component, and it composes through computed and effect boundaries that are easy to reason about. 

import { signal } from '@angular/core';

export class CartStore {
  readonly items = signal([]);

  readonly total = computed(() =>
    this.items().reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price, 0)
  );

  add(item) {
    this.items.update((all) => [...all, item]);
  }
}

The rules stay small: state belongs near the feature that owns it; lift it only when two unrelated branches actually need it; measure before you introduce a dependency.

  • Default to signals inside the component or feature.
  • Lift to a lightweight, injectable service when shared.
  • Reach for a global store for cross-cutting, app-wide concerns.
  • Keep actions near the UI that triggers them.

What stays in a store

Some things genuinely belong in a global store: identity/session, feature flags, capability toasts. Those are shared, coarse-grained and few. Everything else is usually fine closer to home. The refactor rarely removes code — it moves it somewhere better.

If you push back on the next "let's spin up a store for this" request even once a week, you'll ship simpler apps and thank yourself in six months.
